frontend.prompt:
Implement a client-side "undo delete (restore)" feature that uses the new backend POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore endpoint. Do not persist undo state across page reloads. Requirements and implementation steps:

1) In-memory session store
- Keep a runtime-only (in-memory) set/array of item ids that were successfully deleted during the current browser session. Do not write this set to localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, or any persistent storage.
- Add id when a delete operation returns success (existing delete behavior). Only record ids for which the backend delete call returned success.

2) Undo UI
- When an id is recorded, surface a single-item undo affordance associated with that item in the current page context (e.g., a per-row toast/snackbar or a small inline "Undo" button near where the item was shown). The UI must be dismissible and must disappear when the undo is applied or when the id is removed from the in-memory set.
- Do not add or rely on a global "recycle bin" view. The undo affordance is transient and not required to persist after a full page refresh.

3) Undo action behavior
- When the user clicks "Undo" for id:
  a) Send POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore with no request body.
  b) On HTTP 200: response body will be an ItemPublic representation. Replace or insert the returned ItemPublic into the visible list/state so the restored item shows again; ensure the restored item's deleted_at is treated as null. Update any visible total counts/statistics on the page so the restored item is included (increment the count if the UI previously decremented it at deletion). Remove id from the in-memory set and dismiss the undo UI.
  c) On HTTP 409 with JSON {"detail":"Item is not deleted"}: dismiss the undo UI and remove id from the in-memory set. Optionally show a non-blocking notification that the item was already restored elsewhere. Do not attempt further restores for that id.
  d) On HTTP 404 or 403: show an error notification describing the failure (e.g., "Item not found" or "You are not allowed to restore this item"). After notifying, remove id from the in-memory set and dismiss the undo UI (to avoid stale undo entries). If product requires a different behavior for 403/404 (e.g. keep undo entry), open a decision request rather than guessing.
  e) On network/timeouts: surface a retry affordance and keep the id in the in-memory set until user dismisses or a terminal response is received.

4) UI state and counts
- Ensure that after a successful 200 restore the UI list and any displayed counters (total items, page counts, summary counts) include the restored item. If lists are paginated, insert the restored item into the list according to existing sort/filter rules (use the ItemPublic fields returned by the backend to determine position). If it is not possible to deterministically place the item client-side, reload the current page/list from the server after successful restore (preferred if placing would violate server-side ordering rules).

5) Error handling and messages
- Expect response bodies to be JSON. For 409 specifically expect {"detail":"Item is not deleted"}. For 404/403 use whatever error format the API already uses; preserve message content when displaying to the user.

6) Tests
- Add unit/component tests that simulate: a successful delete followed by clicking Undo producing a 200 -> item reappears and counters update; server responds 409 -> undo UI disappears and user is informed; server responds 403/404 -> appropriate error shown and undo entry cleared; network error -> retry option shown.
- Add an e2e test that performs delete -> undo and asserts the item appears and counts change.

7) Accessibility and UX
- Ensure undo control is keyboard-focusable and has accessible label text (e.g., aria-label="Undo delete for <item-name>").
- Keep messages concise and informative.

8) Instrumentation
- (Optional) Emit analytics events for "undo_shown", "undo_clicked", "undo_success", "undo_failure" so product can measure usage. If analytics is required, follow existing instrumentation patterns.

9) Coordination notes for backend
- The frontend assumes POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore returns HTTP 200 with the full ItemPublic JSON and that deleted_at will be null in that response. It also expects exact 409 JSON {"detail":"Item is not deleted"} when attempting to restore an item that is not deleted. Confirm these response shapes with backend implementers and update shared API specification (OpenAPI/Swagger) accordingly.

Do not make decisions about persisting undo state across reloads or introducing a recycle-bin endpoint — the product requirement forbids a recycle-bin endpoint and specifies that undo is not required after page refresh.

backend.prompt:
Add a new API endpoint to restore a soft-deleted item: POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore. Implementation instructions and contract details (do not assume framework specifics; reuse existing app patterns and helpers):

1) Route and HTTP contract
- Route: POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore
- Request body: none
- Success response: HTTP 200 with body = ItemPublic JSON representation of the item, and the returned item MUST show deleted_at = null.
- Client errors:
  - 404 Not Found: if no item with {id} exists (use the same 404 semantics as other item endpoints).
  - 403 Forbidden: if the authenticated user is neither the owner of the item nor a superuser.
  - 409 Conflict: if the item exists but is not deleted. The response body must be JSON with exactly: {"detail":"Item is not deleted"} and HTTP status 409.

2) Preconditions and validation
- Parse {id} using the same id parsing/validation used by other item endpoints (do not invent a new id format). If parsing fails, return the same validation error as other endpoints.
- Load the item by id including items that are soft-deleted. Use existing data access methods that can include deleted rows; if such methods do not exist, raise an implementation decision request instead of inventing one.

3) Authorization
- Use existing authentication middleware to identify the current user.
- Use existing helpers to check ownership: allow the restore if current_user is the owner of the item OR current_user has superuser privileges via the system's existing superuser check. If those helpers do not exist, stop and request a decision. On unauthorized access return 403.

4) Deleted-state check and restore semantics
- The system must have a soft-delete mechanism (e.g., deleted_at timestamp or soft-delete flag). If the item.deleted_at is null (or equivalent "not deleted" state) return the 409 error with JSON {"detail":"Item is not deleted"}.
- If the item is deleted (deleted_at non-null), restore it by clearing deleted_at (set to null) or call the existing ORM/DB restore operation.
- Perform restore inside a transaction and apply a row-level lock (e.g., SELECT FOR UPDATE or ORM equivalent) to avoid race conditions where two restore requests run concurrently.
- If a concurrent transaction changed the deletion state during the restore attempt, handle that deterministically: after acquiring the lock re-check deleted_at and behave as above (i.e., if deleted_at is null now, return 409). Document this in tests.

5) Persistence and side effects
- Persist the restored state to the database in the same transaction.
- Update or invalidate any caches, counts, or search indices that the codebase uses so that restored items become visible again in lists and in total counts. If such mechanisms exist (e.g., summary counters, ElasticSearch index), invoke the existing update/invalidate hooks. If the codebase has no such hooks, document that lists and counts must rely on standard queries that exclude deleted items.
- Emit any domain events or audit logs consistent with other write operations (e.g., record who performed the restore and when) using existing audit/logging facilities. If no audit facility exists, open a decision ticket rather than inventing one.

6) Response serialization
- Serialize the restored entity with the same ItemPublic serializer used elsewhere. Ensure deleted_at is serialized as null. Do not add or remove fields compared to existing ItemPublic schema.

7) Error messages and status codes
- Ensure the 409 conflict response exactly returns JSON {"detail":"Item is not deleted"} (string must match). Use the same JSON error envelope used by other endpoints for 404 and 403 responses.

8) Tests
- Unit tests for the handler covering:
  - Successful restore by owner -> 200 and returned ItemPublic deleted_at=null, DB state updated, caches updated.
  - Successful restore by superuser -> 200.
  - Attempt to restore non-existent id -> 404.
  - Attempt to restore an item that is not deleted -> 409 with exact detail "Item is not deleted".
  - Attempt to restore by a non-owner non-superuser -> 403.
  - Concurrent restore attempts: test transactional behavior so only one request succeeds or both get deterministic responses per locking strategy.
- Integration/e2e tests to verify that after restore the item appears in list endpoints and that any count endpoints include it.

9) API documentation
- Add this endpoint to the OpenAPI/Swagger specification (or project API docs) including all response codes and example ItemPublic body (with deleted_at = null). Update client-facing docs so frontend implementers can rely on the exact 409 detail message.

10) Backward-compatibility and constraints
- Do not add a new recycle-bin/list endpoint (explicitly disallowed by requirements).
- Do not change existing delete behavior. The restore endpoint must work with the existing soft-delete implementation.
- Do not attempt to persist or manage frontend undo state — frontend will handle that in-session.

11) Coordination notes for frontend
- The frontend will call POST /api/v1/items/{id}/restore and expects: 200 + ItemPublic with deleted_at = null; 409 with JSON {"detail":"Item is not deleted"}; 403 and 404 as per existing error formats. Confirm these shapes and update shared API spec.

12) If any required infra is missing
- If the codebase lacks soft-delete semantics, a method to query including deleted rows, or user ownership/superuser checks, do not invent them: raise an implementation decision/ticket to add the missing primitives before implementing this endpoint.

13) Logging and observability
- Log the restore attempt and outcome at an appropriate log level. Include item id and acting user id for successful and failed attempts, consistent with existing logging/audit practice.

14) Security considerations
- Ensure the endpoint requires authentication and enforces authorization checks described above. Do not allow anonymous access.

Deliverable checklist for backend developer:
- Route implementation + transactional restore logic with locking
- Authorization checks using existing helpers
- Proper error responses (404, 403, 409 with exact detail text)
- Update caches/search indices and counts via existing hooks
- Add unit and integration tests listed above
- Update API docs/OpenAPI
- Coordinate with frontend to confirm response shapes and error bodies

Do not assume specifics about framework, ORM, or authentication implementation. If any of the helpers/behaviors referenced are missing in the codebase, open a decision ticket rather than guessing or inventing implementations.
